About the growth model

 The Student Growth Percentiles Methodology is a norm- and
 criterion-referenced growth analysis method.
 The norm-referenced component of the model is the student growth
 percentile which indicates the relative growth a student makes.
 The criterion-referenced component of the model is the student
 growth percentile target which indicates the amount of growth
 required by the student to reach/maintain desirable achievement
 goals in a specified time frame. For example, catching-up to
 proficiency within 3 years.
 The norm- and criterion-referenced components together allow
 stakeholders to understand what is, what should be, and what is
 reasonable simultaneously.
 The goal is to create a durable metric to assist in moving beyond
 debates over what thermometer is best to discussions of how best to
 use the thermometer.

Describing Student Growth

 Measuring (quantifying) student growth is not a simple task.
 Even with an interval (or ratio) scale (e.g., a yard stick), growth is not
 easy to interpret. Consider, for example, height.
 A child might grow 4 inches between ages 3 and 4.
 4 inches is a well understood quantity.
 The 4 inch increase becomes really meaningful only when understood
 alongside the growth of other 3 to 4 year olds.
 Student growth percentiles were developed to provide a growth
 norm to help understand student growth.

Student Growth Percentiles

 Should we be surprised with a child’s current achievement given their
 prior achievement?
 Student growth percentiles answer this question.
 Consider a low achieving student with 50th percentile growth and a
 high achieving student with 50th percentile growth.
 The low achieving student grew at a rate exceeding 50 percent of
 similar students.
 The high achieving student grew at a rate exceeding just 50 percent of
 similar students.
 The low achiever’s growth is probabilistically as rare as the high
 achiever’s.
 Equally rare does not mean equally good.
 Judgments about the adequacy of student growth require external
 criteria.

What Norm Group?
 States generally re-norm growth every year such that each grade by
 content area set of students forms an SGP growth norm group.
 As such, the median SGP associated with each grade by content
 area group of students will be 50 each year.
 Some states (e.g., Massachusetts and Georgia) have desired to fix a
 baseline set of students against which to measure growth.
 Baseline referenced SGPs (because they are anchored to student
 growth from previous years) could have medians above/below 50.
 Calculating baseline SGPs requires at least four years of data in
 each grade and content area built on a stable scale. That is, one
 can’t have scale drift.
 Transitioning to a consortium assessment (SBAC/PARCC) will not
 permit the calculation of baseline referenced SGPs until at least 4
 years of data are available on the new scale.

Going from Students to Classrooms/Schools

 It’s of interest to examine schools/classrooms where students
 demonstrate, on average, extraordinarily high and low student
 growth.
 To summarize the student growth percentiles associated with a
 school/classroom (or other grouping) Colorado calculates the
 median of the student growth percentiles.
 If students were randomly assigned to classrooms/schools, expect
 to see a median of 50.
 Values greatly above or below 50 are of interest in identifying best
 practices or providing extra support.
 Examining growth with achievement sheds new light on
 school/classroom performance.

Going from Students to Classrooms/Schools
 Hawaii is currently discussing how to characterize instructor median
 SGPs as part of educator educator evaluation
 There are numerous ways states are doing this
 Fixed (i.e., SGP based) cuts.
 Adding confidence intervals around the median SGP or building them
 into the cuts.
 Variable SGP based cuts.
 Hawaii is currently investigating approach number 3.
 Hawaii’s approach will always yield the same percentage of teacher in
 the same categories (i.e., like grading on a curve).
 The cuts for the categories will likely change every year leading to a
 communication issue that will likely need to be addressed.
 This approach would not be consistent with baseline referenced SGPs,
 where the desire is to see higher and higher percentages of teachers
 in the effective and highly effective categories.
 Caterpillar plots can help illustrate some design choices.

The Transition from HSA to SBAC

 Some types of growth will still be calculable while transitioning from
 HSA to SBAC.
 In general, norm-referenced quantities will be calculable.
 Criterion-referenced quantities will require some concordance
 between old and new test to be calculated. Hawaii is not currently
 using criterion-referenced growth as part of reporting or
 accountability.
 Baseline referenced SGPs won’t be calculable until multiple years of
 data on the new scale is available.
 States already considering growth during assessment transition
 consider communication across the assessment transition to be their
 most significant difficulty (not analysis).
